problem: Prior instruction-following agents map language and raw visual observations directly to actions with one monolithic policy, often trained by RL. This recomputes the goal at every step, is sample-inefficient given small language datasets, and is not interpretable. Existing 3D instruction datasets were also small in state space, used synthetic language, or (like R2R) had no manipulation.
motivation: An agent usually only needs to identify its goal once per instruction, while it chooses low-level actions at every step. Separating the two lets the language-grounding part be learned with sample-efficient supervised learning and the exploration-heavy control part with policy gradient. It also yields a goal map that a user can inspect before a robot acts. The authors also release two benchmarks to test this: LANI (landmark navigation) and CHAI (household navigation and manipulation).
key_idea: Predict the goal once as a language-conditioned probability map over the initial panorama using LingUNet (a U-Net whose skip connections are filtered by text-generated 1x1 kernels). Then generate actions with an RNN that sees only the projected goal mask, training the two parts separately (supervised for goals, contextual-bandit policy gradient with oracle goals for actions).
insight: Most of the gain comes from decomposing learning and supervising the language/goal part. Training the same model jointly with policy gradient (OA w/joint) drops LANI dev TC from 35.72 to 21.76, below Chaplot18 (31.0). Removing language gives 23.02, and removing the action RNN gives 31.30. With oracle goals, LANI TC jumps to 94.60, so goal prediction (language grounding) is the bottleneck for navigation. On CHAI, manipulation stays near the STOP baseline even with oracle goals (MA 41.07 vs 37.53), exposing the planning difficulty. Goal-prediction error rises significantly on instructions with temporal coordination (11.38 vs 8.24, p=.015) and co-reference (12.88 vs 8.59, p=.016). This matches the design choice that the action generator never sees the language, so trajectory constraints cannot be followed.
method: Panorama encoding: at t=1 the agent rotates 360° deterministically (6 RGB images of 128x128, 60° FOV) to build panorama I_P. A 2-layer CNN0 (128 8x8 stride-4 kernels, then 64 3x3 kernels) produces F0, concatenated with positional channel embeddings Fp that mark which sub-image each pixel came from.
Instruction encoder: word embeddings (32-d) feed a single-layer LSTM with 256 hidden units; the final hidden state is the instruction vector x̄.

LingUNet goal prediction: m convolutions F1..Fm; x̄ is split into m chunks, each mapped by an affine layer to a 1x1 kernel K_j that convolves F_j into text-conditioned G_j. Deconvolutions H_m..H_1 consume [H_{j+1}; G_j] (with dropout 0.5). A softmax over H_1 plus a learned out-of-sight bias b_g gives P_g. The argmax pixel is back-projected to a 3D goal l_g using camera parameters and the start pose.

Action generation: at each step, l_g is projected into the current view as a binary goal mask M_t, with an out-of-sight flag o_t. [flat(M_t); o_t] goes through an affine+ReLU layer into LSTM_A; its state is concatenated with a learned time embedding and passed through a softmax over discrete actions. The action generator never sees the language.

Decomposed learning: goal prediction is trained with cross-entropy against a one-hot gold goal pixel (or the out-of-sight slot) derived from the demonstration's goal state. Action generation is trained with oracle goals by single-step policy gradient in a contextual bandit setting (Misra 2017), with entropy regularization (λ=0.05). It uses a potential-based shaped reward (move/turn distance to goal), stop/collision/verbosity rewards, and Hogwild! parallel rollouts with Adam.

CHAI adaptation: a separate RNN predicts from the instruction the sequence of intermediate goal types (NAVIGATION / INTERACTION), and the model is called once per goal. INTERACTION goals are localized with ray casting instead of ground-plane back-projection. INTERACT takes a cell of a 32x32 grid over the view.

Benchmarks: LANI has 6,000 paragraphs and 28,204 instructions in a 50x50 Unity3D field with 6–13 of 63 landmarks; success means stopping within 5. CHAI has 1,596 paragraphs and 13,729 instructions in CHALET houses with navigation and manipulation. Both are collected on AMT with segmented instruction–demonstration alignment and a 70/15/15 split.

setting.backbone: LingUNet (CNN + LSTM instruction encoder) for goal prediction + LSTM action generator, all trained from scratch
setting.training_data: LANI train split (70% of 6,000 paragraphs, 28,204 instructions total) or CHAI train split (70% of 1,596 paragraphs, 13,729 instructions total). Demonstrations only, no external resources (no pretrained parsers, detectors or embeddings). The simulator world state is used for rewards during training.
setting.observation: First-person monocular RGB (128x128, 60° FOV) + agent pose. An initial 360° panorama (6 images) is used for goal prediction.
setting.action_space: LANI: discrete FORWARD 1.5 / TURNLEFT / TURNRIGHT 15° / STOP. CHAI: FORWARD 0.1 / TURN 90° / STOP / INTERACT at a 32x32 grid cell of the view. Horizon 40.
setting.simulator: Custom Unity3D environment (LANI); CHALET house simulator (CHAI)
setting.privileged: agent pose and camera parameters used to project the predicted goal (part of the agent's observation); no GT map or goal at test time (oracle goals only in an ablation)

numbers_note: Paper metrics are mapped to canonical keys: task completion TC → SR (success = stopping within distance 5 on LANI) and stop distance SD → NE; CHAI manipulation accuracy is kept as MA. Other dev ablations in Table 3 are not listed: OA w/o RNN (LANI 9.21/31.30, CHAI 3.75/37.43) and OA w/o Language (LANI 10.65/23.02, CHAI 3.22/37.53). Human performance on 100 dev examples: LANI SD 5.2, TC 63%; CHAI SD 1.34, MA 100%. Human Likert ratings on 50 LANI dev examples: 4.38 for humans vs 3.78 for the approach. The CHAI navigation-only split is described only as 'train and test data', so the test split is assumed.
results: On LANI test the approach reaches TC 36.9 / SD 8.43. The strongest baseline, Chaplot18 gated attention, gets 31.9 / 8.78, and Misra17 gets 23.2 / 10.23. Goal prediction also beats Janner et al. 2018 (LANI dev Acc 35.83 vs 30.26). On CHAI, Misra17 and Chaplot18 fail to learn (they match the STOP baseline, SD 3.59). The approach modestly reduces test SD to 3.34, a 17% error reduction on navigation-only instructions, but manipulation stays near trivial (MA 39.97 vs 39.77). A large gap to humans remains (63% TC on LANI).
limitations: Cascading errors: action generation depends entirely on a single predicted goal and never sees the instruction, so it cannot follow trajectory constraints (e.g., 'keep it on your right') or resolve co-reference.

CHAI manipulation is essentially unsolved: MA stays near the STOP baseline even with oracle goals, and CHAI needs hand-designed goal-type sequencing and intermediate goals derived from demonstrations.
Goal-based automatic metrics are strict for ambiguous instructions (humans get only 63% TC on LANI). Evaluation is simulation only, in synthetic Unity/CHALET environments.
builds_on: Misra et al. 2017 (contextual bandit policy gradient for instruction following)
